turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on through, take a seat. What brings you in today?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah, not much, really. Heart just does this little flutter thing. I nearly didn't bother coming.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): A flutter. When do you actually notice it?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Mostly at night, lying there. And before an exam, or those Monday meetings at work. Sitting up settles it in a couple of minutes. It's nothing.
[SEG0005] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's not nothing. You've been sitting up at like two in the morning, heart going flat out. I can feel it through the mattress.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): You're exaggerating. It's a bit quick, that's all. I can still talk through it.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long has this been going on for?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Um. Last winter, or the one before? I honestly can't pin it. Maybe around when uni went back, I don't know.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): With the racing, any shortness of breath?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Nah. Breathing's fine. I'm not getting puffed.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain with it, or have you blacked out?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No pain. Never fainted. I'm not collapsing in the street or anything.
[SEG0013] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): You do get puffed, though. Stairs at the flat, you stop halfway. And at night you say you can't get a proper breath till it slows down.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): That's just me being unfit. Well, actually, yeah, when it really takes off I do get breathless. Mostly at night. It's mild, though. Not dramatic.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay. So the breathlessness comes with the fast heart, and it's worse at night. What are you drinking through the day, coffee, energy drinks?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): A bit of coffee. And yeah, an energy drink if I've got a late shift and then study. Keeps me going. Not heaps.
[SEG0017] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's four or five long blacks, easy, and those big Monster cans, most days. And the vape's always in your hand.
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): The vape's barely anything. A disposable lasts me, I dunno, four days?
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Nicotine plus that much caffeine can both push the heart along. How are you sitting with the exams, stress-wise?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm not stressed. People make a big deal out of exams. I'm fine.
[SEG0021] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): You were pacing the kitchen before that client meeting, saying your chest was hammering. You looked wrecked. Sorry, the car's on a short stay, but still.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): That was the extra coffee, not stress. I don't do stress.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any regular medicines? Anything from the chemist?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Nothing. I don't take tablets.

[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alright, thinking out loud. Young heart racing at night, worse before exams and meetings, all that coffee and a vape, a lot of this may be stimulant-related. But I can't exclude a rhythm problem, or the thyroid running a bit quick, just on the story.

[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me have a listen. Heart sounds are normal and the rhythm's regular just now, pulse eighty-eight. Chest is clear, no wheeze. Blood pressure is one twenty-eight over seventy-six.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): See? All good. Probably don't need the fuss.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): The exam can be normal between episodes, so it doesn't clear it. I'd like an ECG today, and bloods for thyroid function.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): An ECG? That's for old people, isn't it.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): It just records the electrical pattern. If there's an extra beat or a fast circuit, we want to see it. And the thyroid test is one tube of blood, nothing dramatic.
[SEG0031] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We'll do the bloods. I've been on at him for weeks to get this checked.

[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): When an episode starts, try a slow breathing pattern. In for four, hold for four, out for four, sitting up the way you already do. It won't fix a rhythm problem, but it can take the edge off.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Breathing exercises. Right. If you reckon.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): And ease off the energy drinks. Cut the coffee back, and the vape if you can manage it. Come back in a fortnight and we'll go through the results.
[SEG0035] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll book the fortnight and I'll hide the Monsters. He'll complain.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, alright. Fortnight. No promises on the vape, though.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Fair enough. Even dropping one or two coffees is a start. Any questions before you head out?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Nah, I'm good. Still reckon it's nothing, but whatever.

spec.situation: Young adult with palpitations and breathlessness, worse at night and before exams or work meetings; downplays stress, drinks a lot of coffee and energy drinks, vapes; friend or partner contributes. Doctor orders ECG and thyroid tests, discusses breathing exercises.
features: denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.
vague_dates: the patient cannot date things ('since Diwali or after', 'last winter, or the one before'); no invented date; a date_uncertain item.

bad.reason: Patient supports mild breathlessness with fast heart, mostly at night; stairs came from family member, not patient.
bad.text: Breathlessness (category=respiratory, status=present, severity=mild, temporality=current, associated_symptoms=fast heartbeat, aggravating_factors=when the heart races, at night, and climbing stairs, reported_by=patient, certainty=certain)

omissions.text: Asked-and-answered negative finding: no shortness of breath initially denied ('Breathing's fine. I'm not getting puffed') before later clarifying breathlessness only when the heart really races.
History detail from family member: during episodes at night the heart is 'going flat out' and can be felt through the mattress, suggesting marked nocturnal tachycardia.
Symptom detail: patient can still talk through the episodes.
Regular medicines history should record explicit denial of any regular or over-the-counter medicines: 'Nothing. I don't take tablets.'
Follow-up/plan nuance: doctor explained that a normal examination between episodes does not exclude the problem ('The exam can be normal between episodes, so it doesn't clear it').

Real disagreement between speakers: patient repeatedly minimizes symptoms and denies stress, while family member reports more severe nocturnal racing, exertional breathlessness on stairs, trouble getting a proper breath at night, and stress before meetings.
